The trigger mechanism above is designed precisely so that being wrong in either direction is cheap and quickly correctable.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Hardware expansion vs. utilisation improvement for our inference fleet

**Background and problem**

Our four A100 nodes are running at roughly 55% average utilisation, but that number hides the real problem: peak demand between 09:00 and 13:00 saturates the fleet, and batch jobs queue behind interactive traffic. Two teams have escalated latency complaints this month, and our p99 inference latency has drifted from 180ms to 340ms over the quarter. The instinctive response — buy two more nodes, roughly £180k including networking and support — deserves scrutiny before we commit. This memo argues we should not buy yet.

**The case against buying now**

The strongest argument is that our utilisation problem is a scheduling problem, not a capacity problem. A 55% average with 100% peaks means we own enough silicon for our actual workload; we simply cannot move it to where the demand is. The obvious fixes are unglamorous: time-slicing and MIG partitioning to let small jobs share cards, a proper priority queue so batch workloads yield to interactive ones, autoscaling our batch pipeline to nights and weekends when the fleet is idle, and consolidating the three orphaned fine-tuning jobs that have squatted on reserved capacity since October. If these changes lift effective utilisation to 75–80%, we absorb current peak demand without new hardware. The engineering cost is two engineers for roughly six weeks — call it £40k fully loaded — versus £180k of capital plus perhaps £15k/year in power, cooling, and support contracts.

There is also an opportunity cost to the purchase. That £180k is our entire discretionary budget for the year. Spent on hardware, it precludes the observability overhaul we need anyway, a second on-call rotation, and the headroom to respond to whatever surprise the next quarter brings. Spent on software, it leaves the capital option open. Which brings us to reversibility: software improvements are reversible and compounding. If our scheduler work disappoints, we have lost six weeks and gained permanenting. If we buy nodes and demand patterns shift — say, a product deprioritisation frees capacity — we own depreciating hardware with a three-year refresh cycle and a lease we cannot easily exit. Buying is a one-way door taken under uncertainty; scheduling work is a revolving door.

Latency deserves its own note. New nodes would improve p99 immediately, but so would better queueing discipline, and the latter fixes the root cause: our latency spikes correlate almost perfectly with batch jobs landing on interactive-serving cards. Hardware masks the symptom; scheduling cures it. Reliability cuts the other way, and I want to be honest about that. Our fleet has no N+1 redundancy — a single node failure during peak hours degrades service for everyone. Two more nodes would give us genuine fault tolerance. This is the one argument for purchase I take seriously, and it is why I am not recommending we rule out hardware permanently.

**Recommendation**

Spend the next eight weeks on utilisation: deploy MIG partitioning, implement the priority scheduler, move batch work to off-peak windows, and reclaim the squatted capacity. Set an explicit success criterion in advance — p99 under 250ms and peak utilisation at or below 85% for four consecutive weeks. If we miss it, we proceed with the two-node purchase in the next budget cycle with much better information about what we actually need, possibly fewer nodes than we assumed. This sequencing is not a delay tactic; it is due diligence. Buying hardware to avoid doing scheduling work is the more expensive way to solve the same problem, and we would still need the scheduler eventually.

**Uncertainty**

I want to flag what could change this conclusion. First, if the roadmap lands a major customer commitment in Q3, demand growth could outrun any scheduling gains, and buying early would then be justified to cover lead times — procurement quotes suggest 10–14 weeks delivery. Second, our utilisation numbers come from our own exporter, which we have reason to distrust; the first week of this effort should include validating those metrics, because we may be optimising against fiction. Third, the reliability argument stands independent of utilisation: if leadership judges single-node-failure exposure unacceptable on its own terms, that is a legitimate reason to buy regardless of what the scheduler achieves, and we should say so plainly rather than dress it up as a capacity decision.

My recommendation, in short: do the cheap reversible work first, measure honestly, and keep the capital purchase in reserve as the documented fallback. We are more likely to end up with the right fleet, and we will certainly end up with a better-run one.

Comments welcome by Friday.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** AI hardware capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've reached the point where our inference workloads are bumping against the ceiling of what our current GPU fleet can handle, and the question on the table is whether we should purchase additional hardware or invest in squeezing more out of what we already own. I want to lay out my thinking on this before we commit either way, because the two paths diverge sharply in cost structure, and I don't think we've fully reckoned with that yet.

The case for buying more hardware is straightforward on its face. Our queue times during peak hours have crept from seconds to occasionally a minute or more, and that latency is not cosmetic — it shows up directly in-facing response times and, I suspect, in the engagement metrics we've been attributing to model quality. New hardware would give us headroom immediately, reduce the fragility of running everything at 90-plus percent utilization, and let us absorb the growth we're forecasting without constant firefighting. There's also a real argument that our time is better spent on product work than on the deep infrastructure tuning that serious utilization gains would require.

But the purchase path has costs that are easy to underestimate. Beyond the capital expense itself — which at current prices is substantial for anything with decent memory capacity — we'd take on more power, cooling, rack space, and maintenance burden. Our ops capacity is thin, and every additional machine is something that can fail and something someone has to patch. More importantly, there's the opportunity cost: the engineering hours that would go into procurement, installation, and integration are hours not spent on the product itself, and right now product velocity is our scarcest resource. There's also a timing risk. Hardware prices and capabilities are moving quickly, and a purchase made today to solve a problem we could solve with better scheduling may look wasteful in twelve months.

Which brings me to the utilization side. Our own telemetry suggests we're leaving real capacity on the table. Batch sizes are conservative, several long-running jobs hold allocations they barely use, and we have no meaningful preemption between workloads. A serious effort here — better batching, dynamic allocation, consolidating the long tail of small jobs, and possibly quantization for some inference paths — could plausibly buy us 30 to 50 percent effective capacity. That's not free: it's skilled engineering time, it carries regression risk, and some of it (like aggressive batching) trades latency for throughput in ways we'd need to tune carefully against our-facing SLOs. But it's reversible, it builds durable capability rather than a bigger bill, and it defers the capital decision until we actually know our steady-state demand rather than our current peak.

The reliability angle cuts both ways, and I want to be honest about that. Running a leaner, more utilized fleet means less slack when something breaks. Right now, a node going down is annoying; in a tightly packed fleet, it could mean degraded service for hours. Any utilization push has to include explicit headroom targets — I'd suggest we never plan above 75 percent sustained utilization — and better failure detection, or we're simply converting a capacity problem into an availability problem.

My recommendation is that we do the utilization work first, with a hard decision point. Concretely: spend the next six to eight weeks on allocation reform, batching improvements, and workload consolidation, with a target of demonstrably freeing at least a third of current effective capacity. If we hit that target and demand growth still outpaces it, we buy — and by then we'll be buying with much better information about what we actually need, which machines, and how many. If we fall well short, we'll have learned something important about the limits of tuning and can make the purchase with a clearer conscience.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty here honestly. My 30-to-50-percent estimate is informed but not measured; some of the gains I'm counting on may prove harder to capture than I think, particularly around the latency-sensitive workloads where we have the least scheduling freedom. And demand forecasts are notoriously unreliable in both directions — if we get a usage spike from a launch, the utilization project could look like fiddling while Rome burns. That's why I'd pair the work with a tripwire: if p99 queue latency degrades beyond our agreed threshold for more than a week, we escalate the purchase decision immediately rather than waiting out the full timeline.

The core principle is that buying hardware is a largely irreversible commitment made under uncertainty, while improving utilization is a reversible investment in capability made under the same uncertainty. When the reversible option plausibly gets us most of the way there, we should take it first — and keep the purchase option warm in case it doesn't.

Happy to discuss at Thursday's planning session.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Hardware expansion vs. utilisation improvement for our inference and training fleet
**Status:** Recommendation for discussion at Thursday's planning session

**Summary**

We are at a decision point. Our GPU cluster is running hot: queue times for batch jobs have crept from minutes to hours, and two of our latency-sensitive services are regularly competing for the same cards. The instinctive response is to buy more hardware. After looking at the numbers and talking through the operational picture, my recommendation is that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation of what we own, and hold the purchase decision until we have real evidence about how much of our demand is genuine capacity shortage versus scheduling waste. I want to be clear that this is a judgment call under uncertainty, not a settled fact, and I'll lay out where I think we could be wrong.

**The cost picture**

A meaningful expansion — enough cards to relieve our current contention plus headroom — would cost on the order of several hundred thousand dollars once you include networking, power provisioning, and the rack space. That is not catastrophic for us, but it is large enough that we should be confident we're solving the right problem before writing the cheque. The ongoing costs matter too: power and cooling for idle or lightly-used accelerators are real money, and depreciation on GPUs is unforgiving given how quickly the performance-per-dollar frontier moves. Every card we buy today is a card we may wish we'd bought eighteen months from now instead.

By contrast, the utilisation work is mostly engineering time. We estimate two to three engineers for a quarter to build proper job scheduling, implement model-level batching improvements, and get honest telemetry in place. That's not free, but it's an order of magnitude cheaper, and it produces assets —ing, visibility, operational discipline — that pay off regardless of what we later decide about hardware.

**Latency and reliability**

The latency argument for buying is the strongest one on the purchase side. Our interactive services genuinely do suffer when batch jobs crowd them out, and no amount of clever scheduling fully eliminates the risk of a training run monopolising a card that a-facing request needs. If we buy, the right shape is a small dedicated pool for latency-critical workloads, not a general expansion.

But I don't think we've earned that conclusion yet. Our current telemetry is weak enough that we can't distinguish between "the cluster is full" and "the cluster is full of badly packed jobs." Anecdotally, we see cards sitting idle between batch stages, models loaded into memory but serving nothing, and jobs sized to whole cards when they need fractions. If even a third of our nominal utilisation is waste, the purchase case weakens considerably. On reliability, more hardware does add redundancy — a single failed card today can stall a pipeline — but better checkpointing and failover would address much of that risk at far lower cost.

**Opportunity cost and reversibility**

The opportunity cost cuts both ways, and this is where I want to be honest about the trade-off. Every dollar and every engineer-hour spent on utilisation work is a dollar not spent on product features, and if our demand is real and growing, we will have spent a quarter delaying the inevitable. That's a genuine risk. Against it: hardware purchases are largely irreversible at our scale. Reselling GPUs recovers some value but not most of it, and the sunk cost is sunk. Utilisation improvements, by contrast, are highly reversible — if the scheduling work turns out to be a dead end, we've lost a quarter of engineering time and we buy the hardware then, with better information. Buying first and discovering we didn't need it is the worse error, because we can't un-buy.

**Recommendation**

Commit to a one-quarter utilisation push with a defined success gate: if we can demonstrably recover enough capacity to bring queue times and p99 latencies within target, we defer purchase by at least two quarters. If the work stalls, or if honest telemetry shows utilisation is already high and demand is simply growing, we proceed with the purchase — ideally the dedicated latency pool plus modest general capacity — with the confidence that we exhausted the cheaper path first.

**Uncertainty**

The biggest unknown is our demand trajectory. If the new product launches land as hoped, our inference load could double within two quarters, and no realistic scheduling improvement covers that. I'd rather we revisit this memo in ninety days with real numbers than pretend we can resolve that question today. I'd welcome pushback, particularly from anyone closer to the latency-sensitive services.

— Infrastructure Team

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Recommendation on our next capacity decision

**Summary**

We are approaching saturation on our local inference hardware. Peak-hour utilization on our eight A100s has crossed 85%, queue times during business hours have tripled since the new retrieval pipeline launched, and two product teams have begun quietly routing traffic to a hosted API as a workaround. The question on the table is whether we spend roughly $180K on four additional GPUs or invest the next quarter in squeezing more out of what we already own. My recommendation is the latter, with a bounded commitment: spend the next ten weeks on utilization work, and pre-approve the hardware purchase only if we fail to bring sustained peak utilization below 70% or p95 queue latency under 400ms.

**The case for buying**

The argument for new hardware is straightforward and not wrong. Our latency SLO is already at risk; the p95 for interactive requests went from 180ms to 520ms over the last two months, and the product team has noticed. Every week of degradation carries some cost in experience and in engineering credibility. Buying capacity is also fast — procurement quotes are in hand, delivery is six weeks, and the fix is immediate once racks are installed. There is a real argument that our time is better spent on product work than on infrastructure heroics.

**The case for improving utilization first**

But the utilization picture is worse than the headline number suggests. Tracing over the past three weeks shows that roughly 30% of peak-hour GPU-seconds are spent on batch jobs that could run off-peak, on models loaded but idle for hours, or on requests that retry after timeouts caused by the queue itself — retries that then double the load. Our batching window is set conservatively from a config written a year ago, and we have never profiled it against current traffic. Memory fragmentation from long-lived model processes is forcing us to restart nodes weekly, which itself creates latency spikes and wastes capacity. In short, a meaningful fraction of our "saturation" is self-inflicted, and hardware bought today would inherit these inefficiencies. Four new GPUs at 85% waste-adjusted utilization buys us far less than four GPUs on paper.

There is also the opportunity cost to weigh honestly. $180K is roughly one engineer-year fully loaded, or the entire annual budget for our evaluationing, which everyone agrees is overdue. And hardware is not very reversible. Once purchased, GPUs depreciate whether or not we need them, they consume power and rack space, and reselling them mid-lifecycle recovers perhaps half their value. Utilization work, by contrast, is almost entirely reversible: config changes, scheduler improvements, and better batching can be rolled back if they misbehave, and the engineering time invested builds durable knowledge about our own workload that we will need regardless of what we eventually buy.

**Reliability deserves its own mention.** Our current fleet has no meaningful headroom for node failure. When one A100 node went down for a firmware issue last month, interactive latency breached SLO for six hours. This is the strongest argument for *some* new hardware — not for throughput, but for redundancy. I take this seriously, and it is why my recommendation is not "never buy" but "buy later, and buy with better information." If utilization work succeeds, we will know precisely how much headroom we need and can size the purchase accordingly — possibly two GPUs instead of four, possibly a different memory profile entirely once we understand our real model-mix demands.

**Uncertainty**

I want to be candid about what we don't know. Traffic is growing roughly 8% month over month, and if the new product launches in Q3 land as hoped, that slope steepens. Utilization work buys time, not immunity; if growth continues, hardware is coming eventually. There is also execution risk: the ten-week plan assumes the batching and scheduling work goes smoothly, and infrastructure projects of this kind routinely uncover surprises. If we discover mid-quarter that the waste is structural rather than configurational, we will have spent six weeks learning what a purchase order would have told us in one. That is a real cost, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. The mitigation is the pre-approved trigger: if we miss the targets above by week ten, the purchase proceeds without another round of debate.

**Recommendation**

Spend the quarter on utilization. Set explicit, measurable targets now. Keep the hardware purchase pre-approved as the fallback, and revisit in ten weeks with data rather than anxiety. The cheapest capacity we will ever buy is the capacity we already own but aren't using well — and the decision we make with better measurements will be a better decision.

Happy to walk through the tracing data with anyone who wants the detail.
